text: At the time, we didn't really have a solid product yet. We would have 10 to 15 meetings every day with potential customers. I was hired as the first product manager. I sat in on those calls.
speaker: Raaz Herzberg
context: Lenny asks Raaz about the early days at Wiz when the company was struggling to find the right product direction. Raaz explains how she joined as the first product manager during a confusing period where the team was having many customer meetings but nobody really understood what they were building. After weeks of customer calls where she couldn't grasp what product they were supposed to develop, she finally asked the direct question that led to their successful pivot to cloud security.
text_ko: 그때는 아직 제대로 된 제품이 없었어요. 매일 잠재 고객들과 미팅을 10~15개씩 했죠. 저는 첫 번째 제품 매니저(product manager)로 채용돼서 그 통화들에 모두 참여했어요. 그런데도 우리가 정확히 뭘 만들 건지 잘 이해가 안 됐어요. 제품 매니저였으니 당연히 그걸 시작해야 했기 때문에 더 혼란스러웠죠. 결국에는 "우리가 정확히 뭘 하는 거죠?"라고 물어봤고, 그 질문이 결국 우리를 클라우드 보안(cloud security) 쪽으로 피벗(pivot)하게 만들었어요.
text_zh: 当时我们其实还没有什么像样的产品。我们每天要跟潜在客户开10到15个会。我是被招进来做第一个产品经理(product manager)的。那些电话会议我都参加了。但说实话，我还是搞不清楚我们到底要做什么产品，这就很尴尬了，因为我是产品经理啊，按理说应该由我来负责产品开发的。所以到了某个时候，我实在忍不住了，就问："咱们到底在搞什么啊？"结果就是这么一问，我们就转向了云安全(cloud security)这个方向。
text_es: En ese momento, la verdad es que no teníamos un producto sólido todavía. Nos metíamos en 10 o 15 reuniones diarias con clientes potenciales. Me contrataron como el primer gerente de producto. Me quedaba en esas llamadas escuchando. Seguía sin entender exactamente qué íbamos a desarrollar, lo cual era confuso, porque yo era el gerente de producto, se supone que tenía que empezar a construirlo, y entonces, en algún momento fue como, "Tengo que preguntar, ¿qué estamos haciendo aquí exactamente?" Y eso terminó haciéndonos dar la vuelta hacia la seguridad en la nube (cloud security).
key_sentence: I was hired as the first product manager.
original_text: At the time, we didn't really have a solid product yet. We would have 10 to 15 meetings every day with potential customers. I was hired as the first product manager. I sat in on those calls. I still did not exactly understand what we were going to build, which was confusing, because I was a product manager, so I was supposed to start building it, and so, at some point, it was like, "I have to ask, what exactly are we doing here?" And that ended up pivoting us around to cloud security.

vocabulary.definition: A product manager is a professional responsible for the strategy, roadmap, and feature definition of a product or product line. They act as a liaison between various departments to ensure the product meets market needs and business goals.
vocabulary.businessContext: In tech and startup environments, product managers play a crucial role in guiding the development process and aligning the product with customer expectations and company objectives.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often implies a blend of technical knowledge, business acumen, and leadership skills, making it a multifaceted role that can vary significantly between organizations.

vocabulary.definition: Potential customers are individuals or organizations that have the capacity to purchase a product or service but have not yet made a purchase. They represent a target market segment that businesses aim to convert into actual customers.
vocabulary.businessContext: Identifying and engaging with potential customers is vital for businesses, especially startups, as it helps in validating product ideas and refining marketing strategies.
vocabulary.nuance: The term suggests an opportunity for growth and sales, and it is often used in discussions about market research and customer acquisition strategies.

vocabulary.definition: A solid product refers to a well-developed, reliable, and effective offering that meets customer needs and expectations. It is characterized by quality, functionality, and user satisfaction.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of startups and product development, having a solid product is essential for attracting customers, securing funding, and achieving market success.
vocabulary.nuance: The phrase conveys a sense of confidence and assurance in the product's value, often used to differentiate between a prototype and a market-ready offering.

vocabulary.definition: The right product direction refers to the strategic path taken in the development and enhancement of a product to ensure it aligns with market demands and business goals. It encompasses decisions regarding features, target audience, and overall vision.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech environments, determining the right product direction is critical for long-term success, as it guides resource allocation and prioritization of development efforts.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase implies a thoughtful and informed approach to product strategy, often used in discussions about product roadmaps and strategic planning.

text: We really felt the type of questions change, right? Silly.
speaker: Raaz Herzberg
context: Lenny asks about the signals that showed when Wiz finally found product-market fit after their pivot to cloud security. Raaz describes how customer conversations completely changed from polite interest to urgent practical questions. She explains that customers stopped saying generic positive things and started asking specific questions about pricing and proof-of-value (POV) trials, indicating real purchasing intent rather than just politeness.
text_ko: 질문 유형이 확실히 바뀐 걸 느꼈죠? 우습게도 통화 내용이 다시 "이거 가격은 어떻게 되나요? 언제부터 POV(Proof of Value)을 시작할 수 있나요?" 이런 식이었어요. 사람은 본능적으로 긍정 확인을 받고 싶어하는 쪽으로 치우치고, 듣기 싫은 얘기를 먼저 들으려 하진 않아요.
text_zh: 我们真的感觉到客户问的问题变了，对吧？特别明显。电话里听起来就是，又开始问"你们怎么定价的，什么时候可以开始做概念验证(POV)？"我觉得这很自然，人嘛，总是倾向于找认同感，而不愿意听那些不中听的话。
text_es: Realmente notamos que el tipo de preguntas cambió, ¿verdad? Una tontería. Las llamadas sonaban como, otra vez, "¿Cómo están manejando los precios de esto, o cuándo podemos empezar a hacer un POV?" Creo que naturalmente, como seres humanos, tienes una tendencia a buscar confirmación, en lugar de una tendencia hacia lo que no quieres escuchar.
key_sentence: We really felt the type of questions change.
original_text: We really felt the type of questions change, right? Silly. The call sounded like, again, "How are you pricing this, or when can we start doing a POV?" I think naturally, as human beings, you have a bias to look for affirmation, versus a bias for what you don't want to hear.

vocabulary.definition: Indicators or signs that suggest a particular trend or outcome.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and tech, 'signals' often refer to data points or feedback that inform decision-making processes, such as market trends or customer preferences.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'signals' can imply positive or negative trends, they are often used in a context where interpretation is key, requiring careful analysis.

vocabulary.definition: The degree to which a product satisfies a strong market demand.
vocabulary.businessContext: Achieving product-market fit is crucial for startups, as it indicates that the product is well-received by the target audience and can lead to sustainable growth.
vocabulary.nuance: This term often carries the implication of a successful alignment between product features and customer needs, and is a critical milestone for startups.

vocabulary.definition: A fundamental shift in business strategy aimed at improving performance or addressing market needs.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the startup ecosystem, a pivot may involve changing the product, target market, or business model in response to feedback or market conditions.
vocabulary.nuance: The term suggests a strategic and often necessary change rather than a failure, emphasizing adaptability in a dynamic market environment.

vocabulary.definition: Exchanges of ideas, information, or opinions between individuals or groups.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'conversations' can refer to discussions with stakeholders, customers, or team members that drive collaboration and decision-making.
vocabulary.nuance: The term often implies a two-way dialogue, suggesting engagement and active participation rather than mere information dissemination.

text: I had a ton to learn about marketing, with what I knew really well, with the problem we solved, and I really knew our audience.
speaker: Raaz Herzberg
context: Lenny asks why Raaz thinks she was successful in marketing despite being new to the field. Raaz explains her unconventional approach to becoming CMO at Wiz. While she had no traditional marketing experience, she had deep domain expertise in cloud security and understood the target audience intimately because she lived in that space as a former customer herself.
text_ko: 마케팅(marketing)에 대해 배울 게 한참 있었어요. 제가 이미 잘 알고 있던 것들, 우리가 해결한 문제와 관련해서요. 대신 우리 청중(audience)에 대해서는 정말 잘 알고 있었어요. 저는 보안(security), 특히 클라우드 보안(cloud security) 출신이라서요. 트위터(Twitter)에서 중요한 사람들은 다 팔로우하고 관련 트윗도 챙겨 보고, 관련 블로그(blogs)들도 다 읽었어요. 웃긴 얘기지만 뭘 중요하게 생각해야 하는지, 지금 무엇이 흥미로운지는 잘 알고 있어요 — 대체로 이게 제 영역이거든요.
text_zh: 在营销这块我要学的东西太多了，但我对我们解决的问题和我们的用户群体非常了解。我本身就是做安全出身的，做云安全的，该关注的Twitter账号我都关注了，该follow的人我都follow了，该看的博客我都看。我知道什么有意思，知道什么重要，知道现在什么最火，因为这就是我的地盘嘛。
text_es: Tenía muchísimo que aprender sobre marketing, pero lo que sí conocía muy bien era el problema que resolvíamos y realmente conocía a nuestra audiencia. Yo vengo del mundo de la seguridad, de seguridad en la nube, sigo todas las cuentas correctas en Twitter, leo a toda la gente indicada en Twitter, y leo todos los blogs que importan. Sé qué es gracioso, sé qué importa, sé qué está interesante ahorita, básicamente porque este es mi terreno.
key_sentence: I had a ton to learn about marketing in my space.
original_text: I had a ton to learn about marketing, with what I knew really well, with the problem we solved, and I really knew our audience. I myself, I come from security, I come from cloud security, I read all of the right Twitters, and I follow all of the right people on Twitter, and I read all of the right blogs. I know it's funny, I know what matters, I know it's interesting right now, generally because, this is my space.

vocabulary.definition: A group of individuals who are targeted for communication, marketing, or information dissemination.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, understanding the audience is crucial for tailoring marketing strategies and ensuring that products or services meet the needs and preferences of potential customers.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'audience' often refers to consumers, it can also apply to stakeholders, investors, or any group that may influence or be influenced by a business's activities.

vocabulary.definition: Not based on or conforming to what is generally done or believed; innovative or atypical.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business world, unconventional strategies can differentiate a company from its competitors, often leading to unique solutions and creative marketing approaches.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'unconventional' can have a positive connotation of creativity and innovation, it may also imply a lack of adherence to established norms, which could be viewed negatively in certain contexts.

vocabulary.definition: A method or way of dealing with a particular situation or problem.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, the approach taken to solve problems or implement strategies can significantly impact the effectiveness and efficiency of operations and outcomes.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'approach' can imply a systematic or strategic method, and is often used in contexts where careful planning and consideration are necessary.

vocabulary.definition: To find an answer to a problem or to deal effectively with a challenge.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the context of business and startups, solving problems is a core function, as companies aim to address customer pain points and improve their offerings.
vocabulary.nuance: The term 'solve' suggests a definitive resolution, and is often used in contexts where clarity and effectiveness are paramount in addressing issues.

text: Marketing is quite the opposite, in my opinion. There's no cost to anything, no maintenance to anything, no technical depth, no anything.
speaker: Raaz Herzberg
context: Lenny asks about Raaz's approach to creating noise and taking risks in marketing. Raaz contrasts marketing with product development, explaining how product features require careful consideration because they consume engineering resources and create permanent complexity. She describes marketing's advantage of being able to experiment freely without long-term consequences, allowing for rapid testing and iteration.
text_ko: 제 생각엔 마케팅은 완전히 반대예요. 비용도 별로 들지 않고, 유지보수(maintenance)도 필요 없고, 기술적 깊이(technical depth)도 없고, 딱히 아무 것도 아니에요. 예를 들어 내일 제가 Wiz의 LinkedIn 페이지에 영상을 올리고 제가 그걸 엄청 웃기다고 생각했는데 아무도 좋아해 주지 않으면, 아무 일도 없어요. 다음 날 다른 영상을 올리면 되고, 손볼 것도 없고 그냥 끝이에요 — 마치 그런 일이 전혀 없었던 것처럼 잊혀져요.
text_zh: 我觉得市场营销完全相反。什么成本都没有，什么维护都不用，没有技术难度，什么都没有。比如说我明天在Wiz的领英页面上发个视频，我觉得这视频超搞笑，结果没人点赞，那又怎么样呢？明天我再发个别的视频就行了，不用维护什么，拜拜，当没发过。
text_es: El marketing es todo lo contrario, en mi opinión. No hay costo de nada, no hay mantenimiento de nada, no hay complejidad técnica, no hay nada. Si mañana subo un video en la página de LinkedIn de Wiz, y a mí me parece súper gracioso ese video, y a nadie le gusta, no pasa nada. Mañana subo otro video diferente, sin mantenimiento, chao, como si nunca hubiera pasado.
key_sentence: There's no cost to anything, no maintenance to anything, no technical depth, no anything.
original_text: Marketing is quite the opposite, in my opinion. There's no cost to anything, no maintenance to anything, no technical depth, no anything. If tomorrow I post a video on Wiz's LinkedIn page, and I think that video is super funny, and nobody likes that video, nothing happened. Tomorrow, I'll post a different video, no maintenance, bye-bye, forgot it ever happened.

vocabulary.definition: The extent of knowledge and expertise in a specific technical area, often involving complex concepts and advanced skills.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and technology, 'technical depth' is crucial for developing innovative products and solutions, as it indicates the team's ability to handle intricate challenges and leverage advanced technologies.
vocabulary.nuance: This term is often used to emphasize the importance of specialized knowledge in fields like engineering or software development, and may imply that a lack of technical depth can lead to superficial solutions.

vocabulary.definition: The process of thoroughly thinking about and evaluating all relevant factors before making a decision.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, 'careful consideration' is essential for strategic planning and risk management, ensuring that decisions are made based on comprehensive analysis rather than impulsive judgments.
vocabulary.nuance: This phrase conveys a sense of diligence and responsibility, suggesting that decisions should not be rushed or made lightly, especially in high-stakes environments.

vocabulary.definition: A method or way of dealing with a situation or problem, often involving a specific strategy or perspective.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, an 'approach' can refer to the overall strategy a company adopts to achieve its goals, such as a customer-centric approach or a data-driven approach.
vocabulary.nuance: The term can imply flexibility and adaptability, as different situations may require different approaches, and it is often used to highlight innovative or unconventional methods.

vocabulary.definition: The possibility of loss, damage, or any other negative outcome that may arise from a decision or action.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business and finance, 'risk' is a critical factor that organizations must assess and manage, influencing investment decisions, project planning, and overall strategy.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'risk' often carries a negative connotation, it can also imply opportunity; calculated risks can lead to significant rewards, making it essential to differentiate between acceptable and unacceptable risks.

text: Almost every single thing I've done in my career, in some ways, even before, I never thought I was going to be successful in it. I guess there's a lot of times, it's a lot of talk about being more confident than yourself.
speaker: Raaz Herzberg
context: Lenny asks Raaz about her mindset regarding failure and risk-taking throughout her career. Raaz shares her contrarian approach to confidence and imposter syndrome. Rather than trying to build false confidence, she embraces the expectation of failure while still taking on challenging opportunities. She explains how this mindset actually liberates her to take bigger risks and attempt things outside her comfort zone.
text_ko: 제 경력에서 해온 거의 모든 일들, 심지어 그 전의 일들도 어떤 면에선 제가 성공할 거라고 생각해본 적이 거의 없어요. 사람들한테는 자기 자신보다 더 자신감을 가지라는 얘기가 많지만, 솔직히 제겐 그게 현실적인 선택인지 잘 모르겠어요. 저는 오히려 뭔가 실패할 가능성이 꽤 높다고 확신해도, 그래도 시도하는 편이에요.
text_zh: 我职业生涯做过的几乎每一件事，甚至更早的时候，我从来没觉得自己会成功。大家总是说要对自己更有信心，但说实话，至少对我来说，我不太确定这真的管用。我只知道，即使我很可能会搞砸，我也还是愿意去试试。
text_es: Prácticamente todo lo que he hecho en mi carrera, de alguna manera, incluso desde antes, nunca pensé que iba a tener éxito. Supongo que muchas veces se habla mucho de tener más confianza en uno mismo. No sé, al menos para mí, no sé si eso realmente es una opción, ¿sabes? Lo que sí sé es que estoy bastante tranquilo con estar casi seguro de que voy a fracasar en algo, y aun así intentarlo.
key_sentence: I never thought I was going to be successful in it.
original_text: Almost every single thing I've done in my career, in some ways, even before, I never thought I was going to be successful in it. I guess there's a lot of times, it's a lot of talk about being more confident than yourself. I don't know, at least for me, I don't really know if that's a real option, okay? I just know that I'm kind of okay with being pretty sure I'm going to fail at something, and still attempting it.

vocabulary.definition: A mindset is a set of beliefs or attitudes that shape how an individual thinks, feels, and behaves in various situations.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business, a growth mindset is often emphasized as it encourages employees to embrace challenges and learn from failures, fostering innovation and adaptability.
vocabulary.nuance: While 'mindset' generally refers to one's mental state, it can imply a fixed or growth orientation, depending on the context.

vocabulary.definition: Confidence is the belief in one's abilities, qualities, and judgment, often leading to assertive behavior and decision-making.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the workplace, confidence can enhance leadership effectiveness, improve team dynamics, and drive successful negotiations.
vocabulary.nuance: While confidence is generally viewed positively, overconfidence can lead to poor decision-making and risk underestimating challenges.

vocabulary.definition: Imposter syndrome is a psychological pattern where an individual doubts their accomplishments and has a persistent fear of being exposed as a 'fraud'.
vocabulary.businessContext: In professional environments, imposter syndrome can hinder career advancement and affect job performance, especially among high-achieving individuals.
vocabulary.nuance: While it is common among many professionals, discussing imposter syndrome can sometimes be seen as a sign of weakness, making it a sensitive topic.

vocabulary.definition: Risk-taking refers to the willingness to engage in actions that involve uncertainty and potential loss in pursuit of a desired outcome.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the startup world, calculated risk-taking is essential for innovation and growth, as it often leads to new opportunities and competitive advantages.
vocabulary.nuance: While risk-taking is often celebrated in entrepreneurial contexts, excessive or reckless risk-taking can lead to significant setbacks and failures.

text: Every time you write something, I wanted to not assume knowledge about Wiz, or knowledge about the product, or deep knowledge about the market. I'll give just a simple example.
speaker: Raaz Herzberg
context: Lenny asks about Raaz's concept of the 'dummy explanation' and how to avoid assuming too much knowledge in marketing communications. Raaz explains her philosophy of avoiding insider jargon and technical terminology that only people within the company would understand. She gives a specific example of how even mentioning their own 'Wiz Graph Database' assumes knowledge that external audiences wouldn't have, emphasizing the need to communicate in universally understandable terms.
text_ko: 무언가를 쓸 때마다 독자가 Wiz를 알고 있다고 가정하거나 제품이나 시장에 대해 깊이 아는 사람이라고 생각하고 싶지 않았어요. 간단한 예를 하나 들게요. Wiz 자체가, 그리고 Wiz가 시장에 가져온 깊은 혁신의 일부는—확장을 가능하게 한 핵심은—그래프 데이터베이스(graph database)를 기반으로 한 상관성이 매우 높은 신호(highly correlated signal)였어요. 그래서 Wiz 안에는 보안용으로 Wiz 그래프 데이터베이스(Wiz Graph Database)가 있어요. 만약 글에 그냥 'The Wiz Graph Database'라고만 쓰면 저는 좋아하지 않아요. 보통 사람이 그게 Wiz 그래프 데이터베이스라는 걸 왜 알겠어요?
text_zh: 每次你写东西的时候，我希望你不要假设别人了解Wiz，或者了解我们的产品，或者对这个市场有很深的了解。我举个简单的例子。Wiz本身基于一个很核心的创新，这个创新让Wiz能够做到现在的规模，就是基于图数据库(graph database)的高相关性信号。所以在Wiz内部，我们有专门用于安全的Wiz图数据库(Wiz Graph Database)。如果你写东西直接说"Wiz图数据库(Wiz Graph Database)"，我不喜欢这样。因为普通人怎么会知道什么是Wiz图数据库(Wiz Graph Database)，对吧？
text_es: Cada vez que escribas algo, quería que no dieras por sentado que la gente conoce Wiz, o que conoce el producto, o que tiene conocimiento profundo del mercado. Te voy a dar un ejemplo sencillo. Wiz en sí está basado en, parte de la innovación profunda que Wiz trajo al mercado y que permitió la escala, fue una señal altamente correlacionada que se basa en una base de datos de grafos (graph database). Entonces dentro de Wiz, tenemos la base de datos de grafos de Wiz, para seguridad. Si escribes algo que dice "la Base de Datos de Grafos de Wiz", no me gusta. Porque ¿por qué una persona común va a saber que es la Base de Datos de Grafos de Wiz, ¿verdad?
key_sentence: Don't assume knowledge about Wiz or its deep innovation.
original_text: Every time you write something, I wanted to not assume knowledge about Wiz, or knowledge about the product, or deep knowledge about the market. I'll give just a simple example. Wiz itself is based on, part of the deep innovation that Wiz brought to the market that enabled the scale, was a very high correlated signal that's based on a graph database. So inside Wiz, we have the Wiz graph database, for security. If you write something that says, the Wiz Graph Database, I don't like it. Because why would a common person know it is the Wiz Graph Database, right?

vocabulary.definition: To take for granted or accept something as true without proof or verification.
vocabulary.businessContext: In business settings, assuming can lead to miscommunication or misalignment if team members do not share the same understanding of a project or concept.
vocabulary.nuance: While assuming can streamline decision-making, it is often better to verify information to avoid potential pitfalls.

vocabulary.definition: The information, understanding, or skills acquired through experience or education.
vocabulary.businessContext: In the business world, knowledge is critical for informed decision-making, strategy development, and competitive advantage.
vocabulary.nuance: Knowledge can be both explicit, such as documented information, and tacit, which is more intuitive and experience-based.

vocabulary.definition: Specialized language or terminology used by a particular group that may not be easily understood by outsiders.
vocabulary.businessContext: In industries like tech or finance, insider jargon can facilitate communication among professionals but may alienate clients or new employees.
vocabulary.nuance: While insider jargon can enhance efficiency among experts, it should be used cautiously to ensure clarity for all stakeholders.

vocabulary.definition: The various methods and channels used by a company to convey messages about its products or services to its target audience.
vocabulary.businessContext: Effective marketing communications are essential for building brand awareness, engaging customers, and driving sales in competitive markets.
vocabulary.nuance: This term encompasses a broad range of activities, from advertising to public relations, and should be strategically aligned with overall business goals.
